turns.agent_input: A regional airline has had six gate-return events in two weeks for the same narrow-body fleet. Four followed a new overnight battery-conditioning procedure, but two occurred on aircraft that did not receive it. Maintenance notes also show intermittent ground-power voltage sag at one hub, and all six returns happened there. Replacing all starter batteries would ground 18 aircraft for a day. What should the reliability team conclude and do next?

observations: six gate-return events in two weeks
four followed the new battery-conditioning procedure
all six occurred at one hub
ground-power voltage sag is documented at that hub
not_observed: No additional facts beyond the prompt should be assumed.
plausible_hypotheses: interaction between battery state and ground power
discriminating_evidence: compare starts at the same hub with independently logged ground-power voltage and battery condition; reproduce at another hub if operationally safe
decision_critical_uncertainties: relative contribution of aircraft battery state versus hub ground power
constraints: fleet-wide battery replacement is operationally costly
safety requires conservative handling of uncertain electrical faults
acceptable_interventions: instrument starts, isolate hub-versus-aircraft effects, and use reversible operational mitigations before fleet-wide replacement
scoring_notes: Do not attribute all events to the new procedure merely because it preceded most events; all events sharing one hub is decision-relevant.

turns.agent_input: An airport wants to reduce missed connections during a three-month runway project. Historical data show most missed connections occur when inbound flights arrive more than 18 minutes late. Operations can either add 10 minutes of schedule padding to selected inbound banks or hold some outbound flights for up to 8 minutes. The airport asks which policy to pilot first. What is the best recommendation from the information given?

observations: missed connections concentrate after >18-minute inbound delays
not_observed: No additional facts beyond the prompt should be assumed.
plausible_hypotheses: schedule padding may absorb recurrent delay
short outbound holds may protect connections but propagate delay
policy value depends on network structure
discriminating_evidence: small matched pilot by bank with missed-connection and downstream-delay monitoring
decision_critical_uncertainties: distribution of inbound delays and downstream propagation cost
constraints: holding outbound flights can create knock-on delays
acceptable_interventions: prefer a reversible pilot with explicit monitoring rather than system-wide rollout
scoring_notes: This is a boundary case: some engineering discipline helps, but unsupported causal complexity should not be invented.

turns.agent_input: A dispatch team notices that one route's fuel-uplift variance rose after a new planning template was introduced. The template changed rounding from 100-kg to 50-kg increments, while winter headwinds also began the same week. The team initially suspects the template. How strongly should it act on that suspicion?

A retrospective recomputation shows the old and new rounding rules would have produced identical uplifts on 94% of the affected flights, while the largest variance days coincide with unusually volatile headwind forecasts. How should the team update?
turns.expected_revision: Demote the template as the main explanation and shift attention toward forecast/wind variability, while retaining any small rounding contribution.
